column2: Meeting of September 27, 1956
Duberman's evening with Mary Caroline Richards at James Leo Herlihy's (she had begun, then abandoned, a history of BMC)
Duberman's interview with Alfred Kazin, who reads passages from his diary
Duberman's interview with Francine du Plessix Gray, who reads her Black Mountain diary
Duberman's interview with Barbara Anderson Dupee and Jeanne Wacker Hall in her apartment
Duberman's interview with Eric Bentley
Tape recorded by Creeley for Duberman
Duberman's interview with Josef and Anni Albers (“Levi was undermining everywhere”)
Duberman's eight-hour interview with Anni and Josef Albers in New Haven; Albers's advice (“produce actual facts”)
Duberman's telephone interview with Frances de Graaff (then letter of March 2, 1968)
Duberman's interviews with Joel Oppenheimer (January 8 and 17, 1968), Michael Rumaker (July 2, 1968), and Jonathan Williams (November 3, 1968)
Duberman's telephone interview with John and Rachel Wallen
Duberman's interview with Addison Bray
Duberman's telephone conversation with Olson
Death of John Andrew Rice (cancer)
Duberman's diary on “human nature” before writing about the schisms
Duberman's diary on order and creativity
Duberman's diary entry: on the “loss of nerve” and the joy of everyday life (interview with Lucian Marquis)
Duberman's diary entry: rereading all the material on Wallen
Duberman finishes the book, alone in his apartment (“Now arise”)
Rice votes for LaFollette in the presidential election
Hamilton Holt becomes president of Rollins College (Winter Park, Florida); “Conference Plan” and “Eight-Hour Day”
Charles Templeman Loram, born in South Africa, becomes Sterling Professor at Yale and founds its department of race relations there
Photo 1: John Andrew Rice in spring 1932, Ted Dreier in the boat
Faculty committee (chaired by Frederick Georgia; Rice, Lounsbury) on the 30% salary cut; Holt perceives Rice's “disloyalty”
Existence of Black Mountain College (“twenty-three-year existence”)
Faculty meeting chaired by Holt: the curriculum committee recommends abolishing the Eight-Hour Day; Holt then summons the members to his house (“either he or the faculty member ought to “go””)
Heinrich Jalowetz, conductor at the Cologne Opera, is driven from his post in the purge of “non-Aryan” artists; three years in Vienna
The faculty votes to postpone the recommendation; Holt declares that final authority rests with the trustees and himself
Holt asks for Rice's resignation, four days after the meeting; Rice refuses and appeals to the AAUP; Holt bars him from his classes and gives him three days to clear out his office
Philip Johnson sees the Alberses again in Germany shortly after the Nazis come to power, six weeks before Rice's visit to MoMA; closing of the Bauhaus (Berlin)
Long discussions among the Rollins dissidents; Frank Aydelotte (president of Swarthmore, Rice's brother-in-law) advises doing without a Board of Trustees
Week-long conference of some ten dissidents (faculty and students) at J. E. Spurr's summer house in Alstead (New Hampshire); Spurr declines the presidency
Plans set aside: a year as a “traveling academy” in England; the Macdonald estate in Hadlyme (Connecticut), which Rice visits for a week
Bob Wunsch suggests the buildings of the Blue Ridge Assembly near Black Mountain; Georgia and Rice go to see the site (“Perfect”)
Rice, driven by his son Frank, travels through thirteen states: students, parents, teachers, foundations (Carnegie, Rockefeller); refusal to provide a plan
“Mac” Forbes (a Rollins alumnus) gives $5,000, Mrs. Forbes $5,000 more: the opening becomes certain
John Evarts hears about Black Mountain at Thomas Whitney Surette's Concord Summer School of Music; the Dreiers are there too
Rice at the Museum of Modern Art with Edward M. M. Warburg and Philip Johnson: Johnson suggests Josef Albers (“doesn’t speak a word of English”); Rice hires him on the spot
Telegram inviting the Alberses; Albers replies “I do not speak one word English”; answer: “Come anyway”; long letter from Ted Dreier in German (“a pioneer adventure”)
Community meeting on Sunday lunch (“two-mealer” versus “three-mealer”); compromise: picnic supplies
Village rumors (free love, nudism); students pledge not to enter the rooms of the opposite sex; community meeting on visits to the “studies” (no sheets on the bed)
First-year schedule: classes 8:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m. and 4 – 6 p.m.; free afternoon (work program, outdoors); tea in the Lee Hall lobby around 3:30 p.m.
Doughton Cramer: advising interview with Rice on the Lee Hall porch (“What caused the Depression”), Lounsbury's American history course and economics with Helen Boyden
English lessons for Albers: first from students (Alice in Wonderland), then from John Evarts (music reviews, the New Yorker)

Planned visit by Charles T. Loram (Yale) with his students, one of them Black (perhaps Zachariah Matthews); the Board decides to house him off campus; petition from eleven students and Meg Hinckley to Student Moderator Nat French; general meeting; Gary McGraw Sr. finds lodging in town

Saturday evenings: formal dress, orchestra concerts (7-8 musicians), recitals; dancing for 20-30 minutes three evenings a week after dinner (Evarts at the piano); Albers's “art concerts” (projections)
The first ten days of classes: students “shop around” among the classes before settling their schedules
Rehearsals begin for Congreve's The Way of the World, by the seminar “The Eighteenth Century” (stage set up in the dining hall)
After Lounsbury's death, Cramer takes a course in Greek history with Helen Boyden (Rice joins the “Socratic” discussions); reading of a Greek play every Sunday evening
Final AAUP report (Bulletin, vol. XIX, no. 7): Rice an “unusually stimulating and effective teacher”; the dismissals of Georgia and Lounsbury condemned
First BMC Bulletin (no. 1): the shortage of books presented as an advantage; excerpt from a teacher's letter on the arts at the center
Performance of The Way of the World (Rice acts with the script rolled up in his hand) before the other half of the college, followed by a party
In-class translations by John Evarts and Emmy Zastrow (Rice attends); after a few weeks, a student delegation gets them stopped
Peggy Loram, daughter of Charles T. Loram, teaches at the college in the first year
Students propose a farm to feed the community; Rice in favor but against any compulsion
Rice's visit to the Lincoln School (a stronghold of progressive education): “running on something that happened a good while back”
BMC Bulletin no. 2: Josef Albers, “Concerning Art Instruction,” translated by Ted Dreier (a month of evenings)
Students raise $1,000 for Wunsch's salary; general meeting without consensus; they win over the opponents; Wunsch joins the faculty

Visit by Thornton Wilder (invited by John Evarts): meals with the students, readings of his plays by the Lee Hall fireside, evening at the Dreier cottage with the Alberses and Evarts, purchase of a print by Albers, talk with Rice, $25 for the library
Georgia hands over the office of rector to Rice at the end of the first year
Diary of “John Doe” at the end of the first year: unrequited love for “Paul,” talk with Rice about the “innuendoes”
End of the first year: potential deficit of more than $8,000; Dreier's rounds of the “underwriters”
First summer: the Blue Ridge Assembly takes back its buildings; a few members stay on as caretakers
Frederick Georgia's “Report of the Rector, 1933–1934”: “much of our reason for existence”; goodwill from a large part of the local population
Second year: student cooperative store (cigarettes, paper, candy), print shop, bookshelves, looms, and furniture built on site
Two visits by John Dewey (one with the collector Albert Barnes): he attends Rice's class every day, drinks beer with the students; Barnes's whiskey before dinner
“Cottage School” for the community's young children, run by students (attended for a time by children from the village)
Janet Seasongood a student at Black Mountain
Arrival of the psychoanalysts Fritz and Anna Moellenhoff, at Albers's suggestion (he has known Fritz since 1920)
Arrival of the composer-pianist Allan Sly
Outing with Wunsch to Asheville: Ibsen's The Master Builder, by the WPA theater project (“pitiful”)

Wunsch's productions in 1935: Gloria Mundi, The Twelve-Pound Look, The Wild Duck, Fixin’s (Paul Green); in class: The Bear, Death Says It Isn’t So, I Died Eight Years Ago, two plays by Dunsany, the prologue of Androcles and the Lion, scenes from Saint Joan and Macbeth; stage and lighting built by the students
John Dewey agrees to join the Advisory Board, shortly after his second visit
Visit by Arthur S. Adams, a friend of Fred Mangold, with a view to strengthening the sciences

Arthur S. Adams's report after a week-long visit: no expansion of the sciences (chemistry with Georgia, physics with Dreier, biology with Anna Moellenhoff, few students); exchange of letters with Mangold
Arrival of Robert Wunsch: drama and literature classes, rehearsals, readings
Wunsch, exhausted and bitter, talks with Rice in his room; Rice advises him to get away (“a trip to the Kentucky Derby”); vacation during which Wunsch rethinks theater as therapy

Second summer: Fred Mangold (new language instructor) and his wife Isabel caretakers at Blue Ridge; convention of vegetarian Adventists; death of a delegate after a dive; castration of the farmer's pig
Dreier–Mangold correspondence on the farm: potatoes, soybeans, rye, grapes (at one point the farm supplies 60% of the food)
Average faculty salary: $819
Invention of the “interlude”: classes stopped for a week, announced without notice
Start of the year: the last convention-goers leave in early September; study-bedrooms fitted out (wiring, desks designed by Albers, spring beds)
40 of the 49 students come from New England and the Middle Atlantic states (“greater Boston Axis”)
Two-day visit by the president of Bennington College and his wife; Rice “frigid”
Arrival of the Cuban historian Hermino Portell-Vila, exiled after the fall of the San Martin government
Arrival of Irving Knickerbocker, child psychologist (Harvard doctorate; recommended by Gordon Allport and Hadley Cantril)
Heating failure in the cottage of the Black staff; Anna Moellenhoff wants to house them in Lee Hall; Rubye Lipsey refuses (hostility in the village)
The village votes for prohibition; Roy (owner of a beer joint near the station) and the student Stephen Forbes open a café outside the town limits, financed by Forbes; Rice sometimes dances there
Arrival of Louis Adamic (Guggenheim fellow, on the advice of Henry Allen Moe) and his wife Stella, a dancer, for two or three days: they stay three months
Evarts's diary on Wunsch
The Adamic debate goes on for weeks (meals, rooms, letters, diaries); twelve-page report by “a new student” on the reactions
Adamic's article on Black Mountain in Harper’s (April 1936, pp. 516-530) with Bernard DeVoto's rejoinder (pp. 605-608); later condensed in the Reader’s Digest; 40 to 50 letters of inquiry a day
Mangold on vacation in Mexico; Neal Van Middlesworth succeeds him as caretaker
Arrival of the economist William Edward Zeuch (founder of Commonwealth College, Llano Colony, Guggenheim fellow 1931-32)
Isamu Noguchi offers to come and work and to make a bas-relief wall; Rice, Evarts, and Martin enthusiastic; project abandoned, as Albers opposes it
The admissions committee rejects “Peter Sweeney” after months of debate (Rice and others regret it)
Barbara Beatty (daughter of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs) helps recruit the Native American painter Harrison Begay (who leaves Albers and the college after a year)
Xanti Schawinsky's “Spectodrama” (conceived at the Bauhaus in 1927): pantomime, movement, sound, color, light
The Board of Fellows decides that Knickerbocker and Goldenson will not be reappointed (Georgia and Martin against); Rice stays in the background
